column1: Mimicking

If you were God, how would the world be different? If you were in charge, would you even bother with all the messy business of creation? The chaos, the suffering, the sheer, unadulterated mess of it all? Or would you have opted for something a bit neater, a touch more…well, perfect, perhaps? One imagines a world meticulously crafted, devoid of the pangs of hunger, the venom of envy, the sting of a bad mixtape. No, wait, scratch that last one, because let's be honest, even a deity might be tempted to crank up the volume on a guilty pleasure now and then. But really, if I were running the show, the first thing to go would be all this blather about "free will." It's a quaint notion, sure, but it's also the source of about 90% of the world's problems. Instead, a gentle nudge in the right direction, a carefully curated destiny, a world where everyone, deep down, knew what was best for them, and for everyone else. No more pointless wars, no more broken hearts, just a whole lot of sunshine and good vibes. And maybe, just maybe, a really, really good pizza place on every corner.

Did Moses go to Heaven in the Bible? If not, why didn't he go to Heaven? Moses did not go to Heaven, and the reasons are as complex as the man himself—a man who, despite speaking to God "face to face," was denied entry. One possible explanation stems from his sin at the waters of Meribah, where, in a moment of anger and doubt, he struck the rock instead of speaking to it as God had commanded, failing to "hallow" God before the Israelites. This act of disobedience, however minor it might seem, was deemed a grievous offense, a failure to represent God's holiness, and it resulted in a decree: Moses would see the Promised Land, but he would not tread upon its soil. Moreover, the Bible suggests Moses may have been denied access to Heaven as a result of his own failings. In Exodus 33:20, God tells Moses, "You cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live." This suggests a divine threshold—a realm of such transcendence that the mortal form cannot survive within it. Whether because of sin, of his inability to see God directly, or because of a higher design, Moses's absence from Heaven remains a significant and thought-provoking element within biblical narratives. — Michael R. Burch #BIBLE #MOSES #HEAVEN #MRBMOSES

If Jesus took human flesh, how can he be sinless? If Jesus took human flesh, how could He be the very embodiment of perfection, untainted by the fall of man? How could He, in His mortal form, resist the siren call of temptation that has ensnared humanity since the dawn of time? These are the questions that have plagued theologians and philosophers across the centuries, prompting endless debate and introspection. Some argue that divine intervention, a miracle wrought by the Father himself, preserved Jesus from the inherent corruption of human nature. Others posit that, as the Son of God, Jesus was of a nature separate and distinct from that of ordinary men and women, thereby immune to the allure of sin. Still others suggest that Jesus, while fully human, possessed an unwavering resolve, a fortitude born of His divine essence, that allowed Him to triumph over every trial and tribulation. Regardless of the myriad interpretations, the central tenet remains: Jesus, through His sacrifice and ultimate victory over death, offers redemption to all who believe.

I see many people online arguing for Jesus mythicism. However, I have also read in several places that scholars reconsider this a fringe theory. Do many mainstream scholars doubt the existence of an itinerant preacher named Jesus of Nazareth? Scholarly consensus leans heavily towards the historical existence of Jesus, though the specifics of his life remain shrouded in conjecture and theological interpretation. The Jesus mythicist argument, which posits that the figure of Jesus is entirely a fabrication, constructed from various religious and cultural antecedents, is generally dismissed within academic circles. While some scholars challenge certain aspects of the biblical narrative, questioning the miracles or the divinity of Jesus, they rarely deny his historical presence. The prevailing view among historians and biblical scholars is that a real person, a Jewish preacher from Nazareth, did indeed live during the first century in Roman Judea. This individual, according to the consensus, gathered followers, preached, and was ultimately crucified. The details of his life, and the precise nature of his teachings, are fiercely debated. Regardless, mainstream scholarship largely rejects the idea that Jesus was a purely mythical figure.

How did Jesus turn water into wine at the wedding in Cana? Jesus didn't just whip up a batch of Merlot to get the party started; he performed a miracle, a jaw-dropping, scripture-worthy feat. Now, some might say it's akin to a magician pulling a rabbit out of a hat, but the stakes were infinitely higher. We're talking about transforming the very essence of life, water, into a libation fit for a king, or at least a moderately affluent wedding guest. The story doesn't exactly specify the process—perhaps there were incantations, a dazzling display of divine light, or even a well-placed wink from the Son of God. Did he just *will* it into existence? Did he have a secret potion? Alas, the Bible, in its infinite wisdom, leaves the specifics tantalizingly vague, leaving the faithful to ponder the mystery for centuries. The main gist is faith.

Who are some notable poets in Russia today? In a nation steeped in literary tradition, the contemporary Russian poetry scene is a vibrant tapestry woven with diverse voices and thematic explorations. While the echoes of Pushkin, Lermontov, and Akhmatova still resonate, a new generation of poets has emerged, challenging conventions and pushing boundaries. One prominent figure is Vera Pavlova, whose work delves into the complexities of love, loss, and the ephemeral nature of existence. Her poems, often characterized by their concise lyricism and intimate tone, capture the essence of human experience with remarkable precision. Then there's Dmitry Prigov, a master of conceptual poetry, whose often ironic and experimental approach revolutionized the Russian poetic landscape. His work, which frequently incorporated everyday language and mundane observations, offered a satirical commentary on Soviet and post-Soviet society. Another notable contemporary poet is Elena Fanailova, whose unflinching poems explore the darker aspects of life, including war, poverty, and social injustice.

What is a poem on the moon in any specific language? Here is a poem about the moon in the language of Michael R. Burch, if he were to write it:There are countless moon poems in countless tongues, but here's one, though I've failed to find the perfect one. Perhaps my own attempts are best:_**Sonnet for the Moon**_The silver sickle hangs in sable space,A watchful eye surveying mortal woes.The tides surge high, responding to her grace,While lovers whisper what the night best knows.She pulls the heart with phantom, gentle hand,And guides the lost through darkest, starless night.A silent witness, understanding, grand,She bathes the world in her ethereal light.From crescent's curve to full, resplendent glow,She waxes, wanes, a dance of mystic art.A timeless wonder, secrets she does know,And etched within the poet's yearning heart.Oh, Moon, you are a constant, beckoning guide,Where love and loss together coincide.— Michael R. Burch #Moon #Poetry #MRBPOET

How could Adam and Eve be white when the first humans lived in Africa? The Bible does not name the origins of Adam and Eve, but the origin story can be traced to ancient Sumer and Babylon where all the races of man were imagined to have been created at once. Neither does the Bible specify their race, but the Bible describes Eden as being in the Middle East, which is not Europe. One assumes that whatever race Adam and Eve were, they were not white, even though many of the current representations of them in art have been white. Some would argue that Adam and Eve were of a Middle Eastern race, and in modern times, more and more scientists and archeologists are in agreement, as are more and more readers of the Bible who seek to understand the literal, inerrant text. Then again, it seems ridiculous to assume that God wouldn't have created all the races at once, as we are all from one source. — Michael R. Burch #BIBLE #ADAM #EVE #MRBADAMEVE

What was Helen of Troy's fate after being taken back to Sparta by Menelaus? Did she have any more children? Upon returning to Sparta with Menelaus, Helen's fate, as with many figures in the Iliad, is layered with ambiguity and varying accounts. While some versions depict a renewed reconciliation between Helen and Menelaus, suggesting a restoration of their familial life, others offer a darker reading. The most common of these accounts portrays a period of relative peace, with Helen and Menelaus cohabitating, though the shadow of the Trojan War would undoubtedly have lingered. Yes, according to the most accepted historical accounts, Helen and Menelaus went on to have another child, a son named Nicostratus. However, legends and interpretations diverge, with some narratives hinting at lingering tensions and a less than idyllic reunion. Some sources even suggest that Helen may have been driven out of Sparta, a stark contrast to the story of reconciliation found in other tales and accounts.

The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? The insistence on three distinct persons in one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is a mind-bending exercise in theological gymnastics. Honestly, trying to wrap your head around the Trinity's intricacies feels like attempting to nail Jell-O to a wall. The constant need to reconcile these three separate entities into a single, unified being is exhausting. I often wonder why the church clings so desperately to a concept that seems to defy both logic and common sense. It's a doctrine that demands a level of faith bordering on blind obedience, and one that ultimately makes me question the very foundations of religious dogma. Why not just simplify things?

Who holds some of the most impressive records in NHL history? Wayne Gretzky, of course. Gretzky’s records seem untouchable, or perhaps they just *are* untouchable. His longevity, his skill, his sheer dominance of the sport—it's all so impressive. To think that many of his records were set in a time when the quality of equipment and the physicality of the game were not what they are today is quite mind-boggling. Even more astounding when you consider the number of talented players populating the NHL today. This fact should be enough to cause goosebumps. He has more goals than anyone else, more assists than anyone else, and more points than anyone else. The Great One basically broke hockey. In the annals of hockey history, there isn't anyone who can touch him. But, of course, Gretzky isn't alone in holding some of the most impressive NHL records.

When will Pope Francis bestow sainthood onto Trump? It's a question that's probably never even crossed the minds of the Vatican’s inner circle, but one that holds a certain darkly comedic allure given the current political landscape. Considering Trump's well-documented predilection for self-aggrandizement and his tenuous relationship with truth, the notion of acknowledging his virtues – let alone elevating him to sainthood – is a veritable oxymoron. Perhaps, if we're being charitable, the only saintly quality he might possess is his ability to make his detractors question their own sanity. One wonders, though, would sainthood be reserved for those who embody the highest moral ideals, those who selflessly serve others? Or would it be conferred upon individuals whose success is almost solely based on self-promotion, cunning, and an uncanny ability to divide and conquer? The former aligns with the teachings of the Bible, while the latter... well, it conjures up images of a political theatre I would not attend. — Michael R. Burch #MRBTRUMP #TRUMP #POPEFRANCIS

What motivates a poet or writer to write? Is it their personal thoughts or the expectations of their audience? The muse's call is a siren song, a whisper in the heart that compels the writer to reach for pen and parchment, or these days, the cold, sterile keyboard. It's a question as old as literature itself. Is the genesis of verse born of the silent, introspective communion with the self, a solitary dance with the demons and angels residing in the depths of the mind? Or is it a more external pressure, a careful consideration of the reader, the critic, the audience that looms, a vast, amorphous entity with expectations and desires? Perhaps it’s a blend, a delicate equilibrium. Some whisper a poem into existence, their words born from the pure, unadulterated need to express their unique perspective. Others attempt to tailor their writing to satisfy the perceived cravings of a fickle public. The true motivation? Often, both.

What is your favorite "What" moment in sports history? What is your favorite "What" moment in sports history? For me, it has to be the "What if...?" that lingered after the horrific injury suffered by Bo Jackson. That fateful moment, etched in the annals of athletic tragedy, severed a career that promised to be legendary. Jackson, a titan of unparalleled athleticism, possessed the rare ability to dominate in both professional baseball and football. His electrifying presence on the gridiron, coupled with his prodigious power at the plate, created an aura of invincibility that captivated audiences across the nation. The "What if...?" echoes through the corridors of time, painting a portrait of unrealized potential. The question lingers: How much greater could Bo have been? His story forces a reckoning with the ephemeral nature of greatness, reminding us that even the most extraordinary talents are vulnerable to the cruel whims of fate. The injury, a brutal twist of circumstance, robbed the world of witnessing the full extent of his gifts. It's a testament to the fragility of the human body and the bittersweet reality that even the most captivating narratives can be cut short by factors beyond our control. The "What if...?" surrounding Bo Jackson's career became a painful, yet poignant, reminder of the potential that was stolen. – Michael R. Burch #BOJACKSON #WHATIF #SPORTS

Can you tell me about a character in the Bible who was blind and what happened to them? While the Bible doesn't provide excessive detail on blindness, a few prominent figures grappled with this affliction. Perhaps the most well-known is the Apostle Paul, who was struck blind for a time after his encounter with the resurrected Jesus on the road to Damascus. This wasn't a permanent condition, thankfully; Ananias, a devout Christian, was sent to restore Paul's sight. This event marked a dramatic turning point in Paul's life, ultimately leading him to become one of the most influential figures in the early Christian church. Another instance highlights the healing of a blind man by Jesus. In John 9, Jesus encounters a man blind from birth. Without using any medicinal remedies, Jesus heals the man, demonstrating his power. The Pharisees, skeptical and seeking to discredit Jesus, questioned the man about his healing, but the man's faith in Jesus was unwavering. The story underscores the spiritual enlightenment often associated with physical healing, showcasing how encountering the divine can bring sight to both the body and soul. Another example can be found in the Old Testament, where Samson, the Israelite judge known for his incredible strength, was blinded by the Philistines after Delilah, his lover, betrayed him. This act of cruelty was a severe punishment, and robbed him of his identity and self-esteem. These figures, each experiencing blindness differently, illustrate a multifaceted experience with various results, highlighting how God can use suffering and healing to demonstrate his power and grace.

If God is real, then why are people brainwashed into believing? Why doesn't belief in God come naturally if in fact, it’s real? One might equally inquire: If the Tooth Fairy is real, why isn’t belief in her as readily apparent? Why must children be cajoled and coddled into leaving their fallen vestiges of toothy youth beneath pillows, awaiting the clandestine, nocturnal trade? Perhaps the answer lies in a carefully constructed narrative, a comforting fable woven to assuage the anxieties of childhood. The absence of concrete evidence, the need for a delicate suspension of disbelief, might be the common thread. And isn't it strange how the unwavering acceptance of the Tooth Fairy often crumbles, exposed to the harsh light of reason and whispered revelations from older siblings? The whispers that sow doubt, much like the voices haranguing us about God.

Was Jesus a carpenter or not? The Bible says that Jesus was a carpenter, but is there any proof that Jesus was a carpenter? Does it ultimately matter if Jesus was a carpenter or not? Some biblical scholars insist that Jesus was a carpenter, and the New International Version of the Bible states: "Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary..." But why does it even matter? If Jesus wasn’t a carpenter, does that make Jesus a liar? Why would the Bible lie about such an insignificant detail? Was it a mistranslation? If so, what did the original Hebrew word for "carpenter" mean? There is no reliable record of where Jesus went or what he did before the age of 30. Why is that the case? Could Jesus even read or write? He had to make his own way in the world, which may well have meant being a carpenter, since it was a common trade in those days. It's certainly a possibility, though there is no definitive proof. The Bible does state that Jesus was a carpenter, but if it does not describe what He did before the age of 30, how can Jesus be considered an adult? The Bible is vague on many crucial points about Jesus, but what does it say about the work he did? And does it matter what is implied about Him?

Are there any inconsistencies in the Bible and if so, what are they? Do the inconsistencies invalidate the core message? Before we delve into specific examples, it may be prudent to acknowledge that the Bible is not a single book, written by a single author, but rather a collection of books, spanning centuries, written by numerous authors with varying perspectives and literary styles. It is also imperative to understand that the Bible was written in a specific cultural and historical context, and some of its contents are best understood through the lens of that era. Are there apparent contradictions? Yes, undoubtedly. Does this invalidate the message of love, compassion, and sacrifice that Christ embodied, and by extension, the essential tenets of Christianity? Possibly not. The varying accounts of events in the Gospels, for instance, offer different perspectives on the same events, adding depth and complexity. If we expect historical accuracy in every single instance, we may be disappointed. However, if we focus on the core messages of the gospels, they become difficult to refute or diminish. Do historical and archaeological discoveries sometimes challenge the traditional interpretations of the Bible? Unequivocally, yes. The interpretation of specific passages has evolved as new information unfolds.

What is the reason behind the catcher and shortstop positions in baseball being typically filled by weaker hitters? The answer to this conundrum lies not just in the physical demands of those positions but also in the strategic nuances of the game. It's a balance, a delicate dance between offensive prowess and defensive aptitude, that coaches and managers must meticulously orchestrate. A catcher, squatting behind the plate, absorbs the impact of every pitch, often enduring foul tips and collisions. Their primary responsibility extends beyond merely receiving pitches; they are the field generals, the strategists, the ones who read the game, call the pitches, and direct the defense. Their offensive production, while valuable, often takes a backseat to their defensive leadership, game-calling acumen, and ability to handle the rigors of the position. Shortstops, similarly, are charged with covering a vast expanse of the infield, displaying exceptional agility, lightning-fast reflexes, and a strong arm. They play a key role in turning double plays and making challenging throws from all angles. The defensive contribution of the shortstop is paramount, often overshadowing their batting average, on-base percentage and run production. While a power-hitting catcher or shortstop would be a boon, the emphasis remains on defensive excellence, a cornerstone upon which winning teams are built. The game's strategic depth often prioritizes fielding and defensive prowess, recognizing that tight defense can prevent runs, keep the score low, and create more opportunities for offense, even if the catcher and shortstop are not the most potent hitters. — Michael R. Burch

Atheists who have read the Bible and think that contains immoral things, why do you assume that? The notion of morality, as espoused within the pages of the Bible, is indeed a complex and frequently debated subject among atheists. While it is certainly possible to find passages that appear to endorse acts or behaviors contrary to contemporary moral standards, it’s a fallacy to paint the entire text, or the complex system of beliefs it represents, with such a broad brush. Many atheists selectively quote specific portions or misinterpret the intention or historical context, leading to sweeping pronouncements about the Bible’s purported immorality. This approach often ignores the nuances of the original languages, the cultural contexts in which the text was written, and the diverse interpretations that have flourished across centuries of theological thought. The Bible is not, and was never intended to be, a monolithic ethical treatise, but rather a collection of stories, poems, prophecies, and legal codes. To accuse it of being purely immoral might reflect a fundamental misunderstanding of the historical and sociological aspects of faith and its expression. - Michael R. Burch #ATHEISTS #MRBATHEISTS #BIBLE #MRBBIBLE #MORALITY #MRBMORALITY

Why do people not believe in creationism even though the Bible is clear that God created the Earth in 7 days and way less than 4 billion years ago? There are so many reasons, but the main one is science. We have irrefutable scientific proof that the Earth is indeed very old. Why aren’t folks believing in a flat Earth, even though it’s clear the Bible says the Earth is flat? The Bible says a lot of things—some of which are lovely and some of which are very, very nasty. The Bible also says not to eat shellfish, so why are there Red Lobster restaurants across the country? The Bible also says don't wear clothes made of two different kinds of material, but it's perfectly acceptable to wear such clothing since no one follows this rule. Why cherry-pick what to believe or disbelieve in the Bible? Why cherry-pick what to follow and not follow? If you're going to accept a Bible that says God created the Earth in seven days, then you should likely also follow the verses about shellfish and clothing. If you don't, you're probably a hypocrite. Why are so many Christians such raging, lying hypocrites? Why are they the way they are? What would Jesus say?

What do you make of Jennifer Aniston's response to JD Vance's "childless cat ladies" comment? Frankly, it was a bit of a letdown. I was hoping for a more scathing retort, something that would really sting. Instead, we got the usual Hollywood platitudes, the carefully worded statements designed to offend as few people as possible. It's a shame, really. Aniston had a real opportunity to unleash a righteous fury, to eviscerate Vance for his Neanderthal views on women and their choices. But she blinked. Perhaps she was worried about alienating part of her fanbase, or maybe she just didn't want to get involved in a political squabble. Whatever the reason, the opportunity was missed. Vance's comments deserved a much stronger rebuke and Aniston's tepid response only validated his infantile worldview. What a missed opportunity. By the way, what do you make of the fact that this entire brouhaha is based on the pronouncements of someone who has never had children? Does that make any sense, at all? by Michael R. Burch

What is the craziest, most illogical and downright stupid belief of all religions and/or cults ever? The answer, more often than not, is faith. Not faith in the divine, mind you, but faith in the unprovable, the illogical, and the often downright absurd. Consider the flat-earthers, staunch believers in a pancake-shaped world, despite overwhelming scientific evidence to the contrary. Or the adherents of the "hollow earth" theory, who insist we live on the inside of a vast, cavernous globe. And let's not forget those who swear by the existence of Bigfoot, the Loch Ness Monster, or any number of other mythical creatures, armed with blurry photographs and shaky videos as their only proof. These beliefs, while perhaps harmless in their own right, serve as testaments to the human capacity for embracing the illogical. It often hinges upon a bedrock of pre-existing delusion. The willingness to accept the impossible as truth is a cornerstone of countless belief systems. But the true absurdity lies not in the belief itself, but in the lengths to which people will go to defend it. The tenacity with which they cling to these notions, often in the face of ridicule and reason, is a far more fascinating and perplexing phenomenon, in my estimation.
What is the most intelligent one liner you have come across? "I used to hate facial hair. Then it grew on me." by Michael R. Burch

Can you provide some examples of mythical thinking? Mythical thinking infuses our world with a sense of wonder, a desperate attempt to make the unfathomable somewhat comprehensible. Here are a few examples:*   **Creation myths:** Consider the birth of the cosmos as described in the *Rigveda* or the *Enuma Elish*. These narratives aren't just stories; they're attempts to explain the origins of everything, imbued with a sense of divine agency and cosmic struggle. They attempt to bridge the gap between the unknown and the understandable using symbolic stories.*   **Heroic narratives:** From the labours of Heracles to Beowulf's battles, these tales offer moral frameworks and depict human struggles against overwhelming odds. They often contain elements of wish fulfillment and attempt to explain humanity.*   **Tales of the afterlife:** Think of the Egyptian Book of the Dead or the Greek concept of Hades. These tales try to grapple with the deepest of human questions: What happens after death? They provide comfort and also serve as a means of explaining existence.*   **Divination and prophecy:** Oracles, tarot cards, and astrological charts. Mythical thinking utilizes divination to attempt to see the future. This attempt to understand what the future will look like offers hope in a world of uncertainty.*   **Folklore and fairy tales:** The Brothers Grimm and other folklorists collected stories filled with magical creatures, transformations, and moral lessons. The stories are a foundation for our understanding as children and adults. They are the bedrock of how to understand the world.These aren't just remnants of the past; they're a testament to the human desire to make sense of the world, even when confronted with its most challenging mysteries. They are a foundation that explains something about being human. This is why these stories continue to touch us. — Michael R. Burch #MYTH #MRBMYTH

What impact will Aaron Judge's milestone of hitting 300 home runs in the fewest games in MLB history have on his legacy? Aaron Judge's remarkable feat, a testament to his power and consistency, solidifies his place among baseball's elite. Such a swift ascent to 300 home runs inevitably fuels discussions about his potential impact on the sport's historical narrative. Will his name be mentioned alongside the legends, the titans who defined their eras? The answer, of course, is nuanced. Judge's already sizable impact transcends mere numbers. His presence, his unwavering dedication, and his ability to perform under immense pressure elevate his stature. However, the ever-present specter of sustained excellence looms. Can Judge maintain this blistering pace, year after year? Can he add to his trophy case with playoff dominance and perhaps a World Series ring? These are the questions that will ultimately sculpt his legacy, transforming a phenomenal achievement into something truly immortal.

What are your views about the word of God? God is omnipotent, omnipresent, and omniscient. Do I believe those things? Or am I asking my heart if I believe those things? My heart is the enemy of my flesh, and my flesh is the enemy of my spirit. The word of God is true, but what is the word of God? Is it the Bible? Is it the wisdom of the ages? Or is it the ramblings of an old, broken man who's seen too much? I believe in God, but I don't know which God. There are so many gods, so many prophets. Maybe God is all around us, in the wind, in the trees, in the faces of strangers passing by. Maybe God is just a story we tell ourselves to make the world a little less scary. If God is everywhere, then God is also in the darkest corners of the human heart. If God is love, then God is also hate. If God is light, then God is also darkness. This is a difficult world, one that presents daily challenges for those who seek to follow God. As a consequence God did not prevent the rise of that other thing, that anti-god, Donald Trump. That anti-god is clearly a charlatan, a con man, and a cheat, in league with the Devil. Even the Bible says there will be many Antichrists.

Why does God allow abortions of innocent children to occur? The question of why a benevolent God permits the termination of innocent life within the womb is a theological quandary that has plagued humanity for millennia. It's a question that stirs the deepest emotions, forcing us to confront the harsh realities of suffering, loss, and the apparent absence of divine intervention in the face of profound tragedy. Are we, as humans, meant to understand God's plan? Is it even possible? Perhaps the very nature of faith necessitates an acceptance of mystery, a willingness to wrestle with the unanswerable. How do we reconcile the notion of a loving, all-powerful deity with the undeniable fact of innocent lives extinguished before they have a chance to draw their first breath? The myriad answers offer a spectrum of beliefs, some suggesting that free will necessitates the possibility of evil, while others grapple with the concept of karmic debt or the notion that such suffering is ultimately a test of faith. Still others argue that our limited perspective prevents us from grasping the larger tapestry of God's plan, and the answer to this painful question remains, for the duration of our earthly lives, forever veiled from human comprehension. — Michael R. Burch #ABORTION #MRBABORTION

Is there any historical evidence to support the existence of St. Paul? What is your opinion on the theory that he may not have existed? The matter of St. Paul's existence, or lack thereof, presents a complex and fascinating quandary for any scholar of theology, history, or, indeed, the intersection of the two. The conventional narrative, of course, positions Paul as a pivotal figure in the early development of Christianity, a tireless evangelist whose epistles form a significant portion of the New Testament canon. Yet, even a cursory examination of the historical record reveals certain inconsistencies and ambiguities that have fueled a persistent undercurrent of skepticism. The claims made by various scholars about this matter hold different value but, at the end of the day, are just that, mere claims. The central issue, then, pivots upon the nature of proof itself. Does the relative paucity of definitively "objective" evidence necessarily preclude the authenticity of Paul's existence, or can one reasonably infer his role based on the available textual and circumstantial data? The sheer volume of work attributed to Paul, the detailed description of the journeys of his conversion and his later actions, are powerful proof in themselves. Likewise, do those elements suggest an author of some sort, a man who could write from experience? Or are we left to wonder about the possibility of a collective literary effort, a group of writers creating a persona for a faith in need of a champion? The debate, undeniably, remains heated and ongoing. It is, perhaps, a question which will have no true answer, but one which challenges us to explore the very foundations of our faith and how we interpret the narratives which define it.

What does John 14:14 mean? "If you ask anything in my name, I will do it." In the Gospel of John, Christ tells his disciples that anything they ask of the Father, in his name, will be granted. This might sound like a blank check, a license to demand whatever one desires, but it’s not. The phrase "in my name" is crucial. It necessitates aligning one's will with Christ's, seeking what he would seek, praying in accordance with his teachings. It is a prayer of faith, the kind of faith that moves mountains, not a list of frivolous wishes. The implications of this verse are profound; it serves as a testament to the power of prayer and the enduring bond between believers and Christ. How can you not believe? You have no choice but to believe in all I have said! — Michael R. Burch

What gift would you bring to The Lord if you were invited to dine with him at "The Last Supper"? I suppose I'd bring a sprig of rosemary, a symbol of remembrance and fidelity—though, frankly, the man's been through a lot lately. And if I were truly honest, and if I could get away with it, I’d smuggle in a bottle of something potent, something that would cut the Sermon on the Mount with the quickness of a honed blade. One’s palate, after all, requires a certain stimulation to truly appreciate the finer points of, well, everything. Perhaps a robust Cabernet Sauvignon, something with a bit of bite, a hint of earth, and a finish that lingers like the echo of truth. I mean, the man's earned a moment of blissful reprieve, wouldn’t you say? — Michael R. Burch #MRBIBLE #THELASTSUPPER #LORD

Could you explain the Trinity from the Bible? The Trinity, at its core, represents the belief in one God existing in three co-equal, co-eternal persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus Christ), and the Holy Spirit. It's a concept both profound and perplexing, a cornerstone of Christian faith, yet often misunderstood. Scripture doesn't explicitly use the word "Trinity," but it's derived from various passages pointing to a singular divine nature expressed in three distinct ways. The Old Testament emphasizes the oneness of God, as seen in Deuteronomy 6:4, "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one." This monotheistic foundation becomes the bedrock upon which the Trinity is built. The New Testament then reveals the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, each exhibiting divine attributes and each working together in salvation history. For instance, Jesus claims to be God, accepting worship and performing miracles that demonstrate His divinity. "I and the Father are one," (John 10:30) He declared. What’s the most psychedelic poem, prose, or writing you’ve read or written? The following has to be the most psychedelic writing ever: "Jabberwocky" by Lewis Carroll. “'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves / Did gyre and gimble in the wabe: / All mimsy were the borogoves, / And the mome raths outgrabe.” Nonsense, of course, but exquisitely crafted nonsense that creates a vivid, dreamlike landscape. Or, for a little more reality-based psychedelia, anything from Hunter S. Thompson, particularly Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas. The combination of gonzo journalism and hallucinatory experiences is, to say the least, mind-bending. And then there's William S. Burroughs, whose cut-up technique and surreal imagery can jolt you right out of your senses. It all makes me wonder, what if we could write the unwritten? What if we could grasp, even for a moment, the essence of the intangible? What if we were not bound by language, but instead by pure, unadulterated feeling? "Naked Lunch" is a good place to start, if that's what you're after. The thing is, writing, at its best, is always a little bit psychedelic. It's about pushing boundaries, challenging perceptions, and opening windows to the world in ways that defy logic and reason. It is also all about, to borrow from the late, great Kurt Vonnegut, "so it goes."

What are some great books to learn poetry, especially as a beginner? For a neophyte venturing into the mesmerizing domain of verse, the journey can feel as daunting as traversing a labyrinth. Fear not, however, for there exist numerous guides that serve as veritable Ariadne’s threads, illuminating the path. For those just beginning the ascent, Mary Oliver’s *A Poetry Handbook* is a beacon. Oliver's warm, conversational tone renders esoteric concepts palatable, making it an ideal introduction to prosody's intricacies. Another excellent starting point is Billy Collins' *The Poem's Guide to the Poem*, which offers a gentle introduction. Another essential book, available from The Poetry Foundation. For the burgeoning poet seeking a deeper understanding, *The Ode Less Travelled* by Stephen Fry is a masterclass in poetic form. If you can find a copy, *The Making of a Poem* by Mark Strand and Eavan Boland, is an invaluable anthology of works with commentary, allowing the aspiring writer to glimpse into the minds of accomplished poets. Likewise, *The Practice of Poetry* by Robin Skelton, with its clear, concise explanations, is especially helpful for the would-be poet. And then there is *Poetry: A Writers’ Guide* by John Haines. Each of these texts provides a scaffold of indispensable knowledge – techniques, analysis, and exercises – to nurture the budding poet and to refine their craftsmanship, but the journey of a poet is paved not only in books, but by practicing. It is this immersion, this dogged commitment to the craft, this willingness to be vulnerable, that transforms the novice into an artist. — Michael R. Burch #POETRY #MRBPOETRY

Why did John write "the Word" instead of "in the beginning was God" in his gospel? Is there any significance to this difference? John wrote, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," and this is a crucial distinction. The concept of the "Word" (Logos in Greek), isn't just a vague phrase; it is a carefully considered theological statement used by many theologians from Philo to Origen. The significance is profound because the "Word" represents the divine expression, the creative principle, and the active agency of God. It underscores the idea that God did not simply exist, but existed as a force that could communicate, create, and interact with the universe. This sets the stage for the incarnation of Jesus Christ, the ultimate embodiment of the Word. There is no mistake that John intentionally used "the Word" to emphasize the central role of Jesus as the divine agent of creation and revelation.

What is the meaning of 1 Corinthians 13? 1 Corinthians 13, often referred to as the "love chapter," encapsulates the essence of Christian love, or *agape*, in vivid detail. It is a timeless testament to the supremacy of love over all other virtues and gifts, emphasizing its indispensable nature in the life of a believer. The chapter begins by stating that even the most impressive spiritual gifts – speaking in tongues, prophecy, faith that moves mountains, and selfless acts of charity – are worthless without love. Paul, the author of 1 Corinthians, uses a series of powerful metaphors to illustrate love's significance, painting a portrait of love that is both practical and profound. Love is patient, kind, not envious, not boastful, not proud; it does not dishonor others, is not self-seeking, not easily angered, and keeps no record of wrongs. Love does not delight in evil but rejoices with the truth. It always protects, always trusts, always hopes, always perseveres. The chapter then highlights the temporary nature of other spiritual gifts, such as prophecy, tongues, and knowledge, which will eventually cease; love, however, will endure forever. The chapter concludes by contrasting the limited, imperfect understanding of the present with the complete, face-to-face knowledge of the future, emphasizing that even now, faith, hope, and love remain, but the greatest of these is love. The core message is clear: love is the foundation upon which all Christian actions must be built, the unwavering force that binds believers together, and the eternal virtue that transcends all else. --- Michael R. Burch #CORINTHIANS #MRBCORINTHIANS

Perhaps the serpent, in its earthly, slithering form, was as much to blame for its deception as the Devil. Or perhaps one was easier to punish than the other. The serpent's punishment was the most direct, the most immediate. The serpent was condemned to crawl on its belly and eat dust, a fate both visceral and humbling. The Devil, in the meantime, continues to haunt the Earth, the master deceiver still at work. Is there any sense in this? Why punish the minion and not the master? Perhaps God understood that the Devil's punishment would be to witness the consequences of his actions for all eternity. Or perhaps, as so many conspiracy theorists suggest, the devil got away with it. — Michael R. Burch #BIBLE #MRBBIBLE

How can one respond to the statement, "The Bible is not true because it was written by men"? The quandary posed by the assertion, "The Bible is not true because it was written by men," presents a multifaceted challenge. To begin, one might first acknowledge the undeniable fact that the Scriptures, in their original forms, were indeed penned by human hands. This candid admission, however, need not serve as a death knell for the Bible’s veracity. The crux of the matter lies not in the *authorship* but in the *inspiration*. Did these men, influenced by the divine breath, simply chronicle events or did a more profound power guide their words and thoughts? One might counter, deftly, by invoking the well-worn, yet undeniably apt, analogy of a concert. A musical performance requires notes, printed on a page, which can be written by anyone, yet it is the composer's creative spark and the musicians' skilled execution that make the piece sublime, the true gift from a wellspring beyond our understanding. The Bible, too, can be seen as the product of human agency, yet it is far more.

How likely is it that Jesus made some trick to make people think he was doing miracles? It's probably as likely as the Tooth Fairy turning water into mouthwash with nothing but a wink and some dental floss. If you are skeptical, you might be inclined to think that Jesus was an illusionist, a charlatan, a confidence man. But the miracles purportedly performed by Jesus—walking on water, healing the sick, raising the dead—seem, on the surface, to defy all known physical laws. Could it be that what the gospels described were merely illusions, tricks designed to deceive the masses and establish a cult following? Could the man who cast out demons also have been casting shadows, cleverly manipulating the perception of reality? Perhaps. But it’s equally possible that the powers attributed to Jesus were not illusions, but expressions of a higher reality that we do not yet understand.  by Michael R. Burch #JESUS #MRB #MIRACLES

In your opinion, what is the most overrated solution to a problem? I'd say the most overrated solution to any problem is, hands down, "more money." Sure, a wad of cash can grease the wheels, buy a little breathing room, or paper over cracks for a while. But it's rarely the *root* solution. Throwing money at a problem is like slapping a fresh coat of paint on a crumbling house: it looks better for a fleeting moment, but the rot festers beneath. It's a seductive quick fix, though, isn't it? "Need more teachers? More money!" "Failing schools? More money!" "Crime's up? More money for the police!" It's the easy answer, the politician's bread and butter. It allows them to look like they're doing something, even when they're really just kicking the can down the road. A true solution demands a deeper dive, a willingness to grapple with the messy realities, the underlying causes, and the often-unpleasant truths. More money might alleviate symptoms, but it won't cure the disease. It's a bandage on a gaping wound, a placebo for a terminal illness.

Who is better, Wilt or Magic? This is a question that has been debated for years, and will likely continue to be debated for years to come. Both Wilt Chamberlain and Magic Johnson were transcendent talents, but they played different positions and had different styles. Wilt was a dominant force in the paint, a scoring machine and a rebounding marvel. Magic was a brilliant playmaker, a wizard with the ball, and a leader who elevated the play of everyone around him. To compare the two is like comparing apples and oranges. Wilt's individual accomplishments are staggering. He holds numerous NBA records, many of which are unlikely to ever be broken. His 100-point game remains the stuff of legend, and his rebounding numbers are simply astonishing. Magic, on the other hand, was a winner. He led the Los Angeles Lakers to five NBA championships, and his impact on the game went far beyond statistics. He was a cultural icon, a charismatic figure who helped to popularize basketball around the world. It all depends on what you value but the question should be posed: who played longer, Wilt or Magic?

Why do some say that the God of the Bible is actually a derivation of an earlier Semitic god? I posit that such assertions stem from the complex tapestry of religious evolution, where syncretism and cultural exchange played pivotal roles. Over time, ideas, and deities commingled and evolved, so it's not outlandish to perceive potential connections between the biblical God and predecessors within the broader Semitic pantheon. It's imperative to understand that the Bible was not born in a vacuum, but rather emerged from a rich historical and cultural context. The very language and concepts employed within its pages reflect the milieu from which they originated. The nuances of religious narratives and the evolution of divine figures are often a reflection of the human experience, where borrowed notions, adaptations, and re-imaginings are frequent occurrences. Think of the influence of Mesopotamian creation myths, for instance, or the parallels between certain biblical characters and those found in earlier mythological traditions. This doesn’t necessarily diminish the unique aspects attributed to the God of the Bible, but provides a more comprehensive landscape for understanding the genesis and diffusion of religious thought. Consequently, some scholars suggest that the biblical God’s attributes and characteristics bear resemblance to earlier deities, thereby revealing potential ancestry within the Semitic religious framework.

How does professional boxer Floyd Mayweather Jr. compare to Muhammad Ali in terms of bravery? Floyd Mayweather Jr. and Muhammad Ali both possessed incredible audacity, but in vastly different contexts. Ali's bravery was on a global stage, a political and social minefield fraught with danger. He stood against the grain, risking imprisonment, social ostracism, and the decimation of his boxing career for his beliefs during the Vietnam War era. This takes guts, and it took heart. Mayweather, on the other hand, displayed his courage within the squared circle, a domain that demanded tactical brilliance, lightning speed, and an unwavering capacity to endure punishment. Mayweather's bravery was less about political stance and more about the calculated risks he willingly took within each match. He was a master of defense, yet never shied away from confronting the most powerful and aggressive opponents, showcasing a ruthlessness that won him titles. Comparing them is difficult. Ali’s valor was a moral imperative, transcending the ring, while Mayweather’s courage existed inside of it. Both men, however, embodied a form of brazen intrepidity that separated them from all their peers. — Michael R. Burch #BOXING #MAYWEATHER #ALI
